reasons.C1: Real detection problem on agent payment rails, but wallets are not shown to be LLM agents; collusion link is indirect.
reasons.C2: Held-out split, permutation test and positive control exist, but labels share rule evidence and independent-feature rule is not significant.
reasons.C3: 17-page report against an 8-page limit; key caveats about label leakage sit among many result files.

levers.C1: Show flagged wallets are LLM-driven agents and run a controlled agent-market experiment where the detector catches seeded colluders.
levers.C2: Obtain independent labels from another team and show significant held-out accuracy on features the labels never used.
levers.C3: Cut to 8 pages with one headline table of held-out results and the label-leakage caveat stated up front.

P6.verdict: Solid forensic pipeline with honest stats, but it is wallet fraud detection more than an AI collusion experiment.

reasons.C1: Testing fines, leniency and rewards on LLM pricing agents against a published human baseline is neglected and policy-relevant.
reasons.C2: Nothing built; plan is careful (prereg, contamination test, positive control) but 80 duopolies plus harness solo in 48 hours is risky.
reasons.C3: Plan, demo table, cut order and fallback triggers are clearly stated; no results to communicate yet.

levers.C1: Deliver the human-versus-LLM scorecard across all four regimes with a clean contamination check and several model families.
levers.C2: Ship the harness validated against the paper's tables and full laissez-faire and leniency runs with seeds and intervals.
levers.C3: Produce the promised four-regime table with intervals and a one-paragraph takeaway per policy for authorities.

H3.verdict: Best question in the pile; I would score it high only if the replication scorecard actually lands.

reasons.C1: Latent-channel countermeasures matter for oversight, but channels are non-adaptive, pre-sprint, and no collusion game is involved.
reasons.C2: Real models, held-out data, text baseline, null controls, shuffled-label probe control, reproduce log 10 of 10; no significance tests.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 makes the headline instantly clear, but 13 pages exceeds the 8-page limit.

levers.C1: Train channels adversarially against token snapping inside an actual collusion game and show whether the countermeasure still holds.
levers.C2: Add adaptive channels, significance tests across more seeds, and release checkpoints for independent reproduction.
levers.C3: Trim to 8 pages and state explicitly which work predates the sprint versus what was done during it.

C6.verdict: Most rigorous execution here; snapping result is clean, though it is carrier security rather than agent collusion.

reasons.C1: Say-versus-do gap on secret price-fixing offers is a useful eval angle, but close to existing LLM collusion susceptibility work.
reasons.C2: Many tests and a frozen preregistration, but zero real model runs and no model chosen yet.
reasons.C3: No report seen; only a README dual-use note and placeholder run folders.

levers.C1: Show a robust say-do gap across model families that existing pricing-collusion evals did not detect.
levers.C2: Run the 60 preregistered games on real models and report acceptance and pricing with Wilson intervals versus the positive control.
levers.C3: Write the report with one results figure per condition and the limitations and dual-use appendix.

M4.verdict: Well-engineered scaffolding with a sensible design, but without a single real run there is nothing to judge yet.
